view: The human denotes humankind generally, across people and eras; the following exception supports this broad scope.
note: Kaʿb specifies Adam and his descendants; Elmalılı emphasizes people of the last era. Some notes also discuss loss or its wording, covered separately.

view: Although al-insān is singular in form, it has collective meaning, so the following plural exception is grammatically possible.
note: The generic reading competes with readings of a particular unbeliever.

view: Qur'an 70:19–22 similarly uses singular al-insān followed by an exception for worshippers.
Qur'an 69:47 offers another singular noun, aḥad, followed by the plural ḥājizīn, illustrating collective force in singular wording.
A poem by al-Nābighah illustrates a generic singular followed by an exception.
The human in loss can mean the unbeliever, distinguished from the believers excepted afterward; in one account this person works outside God's obedience or remains astray until death.
note: Other notes read the noun generically; the disagreement turns on the scope of the following exception.

view: The person in loss is Abū Lahab.
note: Muqātil presents this as an occasion of revelation and gives his name as ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; Tustarī says he lost all his days.

view: The person in loss is Abū Jahl ibn Hishām.
note: Reports variously call this an occasion of revelation or an identification; Ālūsī says the example is not exclusive.

view: The referent is a group of Meccan polytheist opponents, including al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil and al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; one report names two men called al-Aswad.
note: The precise lists differ; this competes with the generic reading.

view: The definite article may indicate either the human species or a particular person already understood from context.
note: The two readings underlie general and named referents.

view: The exception's form supports applying the warning to humanity generally rather than only to named Meccan opponents.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says a particular-only reading would make the exception fail.

view: Al-nās ordinarily denotes humanity broadly, whereas al-ins appears paired with jinn and denotes human beings as distinct from wild creatures.
In the image of a declining day, mankind may denote humanity in the final phase of history.
Khusr means ruin, perdition or destruction.
note: These glosses overlap with loss, but specify ruin.

view: Khusr means loss or diminution, as with capital reduced or wasted; khusr and khusrān are equivalent forms.
note: Ibn Shajara stresses decrease; Elmalılı adds bankruptcy, sorrow and deprivation.

view: Loss may be predicated of a person or an undertaking, such as a trade.
note: Attributed to al-Rāghib.

view: Khusr can mean evil.
note: Attributed to Zayd ibn Aslam or Ibn Zayd.

view: Khusr can mean deprivation.
note: The cited meanings are said to be close.

view: Khusr can mean punishment for sins; the cited Qur'anic description of an affair's outcome supports this sense.
note: Some notes add forfeited family, home or property in Paradise, treated separately.

view: The loss is punishment in the Fire, the greatest loss; some describe it as deserved, lasting punishment or as the nullification of deeds that leads to the Fire.
note: Jishumī also suggests the wording states an inevitable outcome.

view: The loser forfeits their allotted family, home, place, station or property in Paradise.
Loss in this warning belongs to the future life regardless of worldly fortunes.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 3:196–197; Corpus Coranicum emphasizes conduct forfeiting future bliss.

view: Qur'anic loss can encompass both present life and the hereafter, with unbelief increasing the unbeliever's loss.
note: This differs in scope from the exclusively future-life reading.

view: Losers can first forfeit what they value most in this life, even without material impoverishment, then lose their souls and families at Resurrection.
Spiritual loss is loss of faith and attachment to God.
Loss in deeds becomes apparent at the final outcome, while loss of spiritual states appears now.
Loss of spiritual state includes contraction after expansion, veiling after nearness, and retreating to dispensations after choosing a harder, better path.
Worldly pleasures and time's veil waste the enduring capital of innate guidance and primordial potential.
The gravest loss is deprivation of serving the Lord; loss of Paradise and entry into Hell are slight by comparison because worship is creation's highest purpose.
note: Rāzī cites 51:56.

view: Humanity is in loss through neglecting God's rights, pursuing desires and failing to fear Him.
Abū Lahab persists in error until he enters the Fire.
Loss can be worldly misguidance or disbelief; faith changes that loss into gain.
note: Muqātil's version confines the referent to the unbeliever.

view: Human life's wasting is like destroying capital: the self and lifespan are one's greatest assets, and sin or failure to invest them for lasting benefit makes one lose them.
note: Elmalılı adds that a final righteous act can make up years of waste and lead to Paradise.

view: Life is a finite loan entrusted by the Creator to be invested; each breath spends it and brings accountability nearer.
After the loan of life is returned, a person's striving and earnings determine reward or liability at the scales: profit saves and a deficit leaves one bankrupt and punished.
note: The notes cite 53:39 and 52:21.

view: Every passing hour incurs some loss because few preserve their life capital: sin is clear loss, permissible or idle acts leave no lasting gain, and even worship falls short when a higher degree was possible.
Knowledge of God's majesty can grow without limit and deepen awe, love and worship, so settling for a lesser form of obedience is a kind of loss.
Even continual comfort would not stop life moving toward death; each passing breath diminishes life, and obstacles compound that loss.
People miscalculate life by counting passing time as growth while failing to compare what they gained with the life spent.
A cited couplet says each passing day takes part of a person because life is most precious; another says people rejoice at days passing though their remaining life shrinks.
Human happiness lies in loving the afterlife and turning from worldly life, but hidden future rewards and vivid senses, appetites and anger draw most people into worldly absorption and loss.
People generally lose by pursuing immediate desires and neglecting lasting good; unbelievers lose through denial, while disobedient believers lose in proportion to their sins.
note: Ālūsī adds ventures, efforts and lifetimes spent on aims useless or harmful in the afterlife.

view: Loss has degrees: denial of God's oneness and the Messenger yields eternal loss, while evil deeds cause lesser loss; avoiding major sins may bring forgiveness of minor ones.
note: The note cites 11:114.

view: Faith alone does not prevent every kind of loss: failure to act righteously and counsel truth and patience leaves sinful believers exposed to loss, contrary to the Murjiʾa claim.
note: Elmalılı attributes the contrary claim to the Murjiʾa and supports the Ahl al-Sunna position.

view: Faith ultimately saves sinful believers, but those whose sins outweigh their good deeds experience Hell's loss until cleansed.
The human species loses through its commerce, exchanging the afterlife for worldly life; the believer instead spends worldly life to gain the afterlife.
note: Ṭabāṭabāʾī frames belief and action as spending life's capital for gain by truth or loss by falsehood.

view: Earthly life is a test that determines happiness or misery in the enduring afterlife.
note: The note cites 13:26 and 21:35.

view: Earthly profit and loss are small beside Paradise, God's pleasure and the final loss of human dignity.
note: The notes cite 78:40.

view: Worldly loss spreads when humanity turns from God's good and lacks righteous authority; even people professing Islam can stray severely from its guidance.
Human nature's deficiency, injustice and ignorance make people vulnerable to worldly accumulation; only God's preservation and faith spare a small minority from these inclinations.
note: The notes cite 33:72.

view: Because even widespread human loss reveals the need for guidance, messengers teach the beliefs and practices that please God and lead to salvation.
The declaration that humanity is in loss is the answer to the oath by time.
note: Jishumī identifies the wāw as the oath particle; Study Quran says verses 2–3 answer it.

view: Inna emphasizes the declaration of human loss.
The wording depicts a human immersed in loss and surrounded by it on every side.
The lām admits two accounts: people are on a road that leads to loss, or remain in a condition from which they cannot escape loss.
note: The first is compared with 4:10's fire already in the bellies of those consuming orphans' wealth; the second rests on continually spent life capital.

view: The statement can describe a certain future outcome as though already present, just as consuming orphans' wealth is spoken of as consuming fire.
note: Rāzī cites 4:10.

view: The indefinite khusr magnifies a loss whose extent only God knows, heightened by sin against God and His immense gifts.
note: Some call it awe rather than mere intensification.

view: The indefinite khusr can specify an unusual or open-ended kind of loss beyond ordinary financial or status loss.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects limiting indefiniteness to intensification; Ṭabāṭabāʾī compares loss of self and family at Judgment.

view: A minority possibility takes the indefinite as belittling human loss relative to Satan's, consoling people that another is more disobedient.
note: Rāzī prefers magnification instead.

view: The common reading has a still sīn in khusr; other reciters vocalize it with ḍamma, a variation like ʿusr and yusr.
note: Reports name al-Aʿraj, ʿĀṣim or a transmission from him, Ṭalḥa, ʿĪsā al-Thaqafī, Ibn Hurmuz and Zayd ibn ʿAlī.

view: A reading attributed to ʿAlī adds time's vicissitudes or calamities to the oath and says humanity remains in loss until the end of time.
note: Elmalılı treats this as interpretive and links time's changes, squeezing or confinement to the warning.

view: A reading attributed to ʿAlī or Ibn Masʿūd adds that humanity remains in loss until time's end.
note: Qatāda also notes this addition.

view: Ibn Masʿūd's codex is reported to read that God created humanity in loss.
The standard reading used by the community and codices is upheld against the additions attributed to ʿAlī, which are not Qur'an for recitation.
note: Qurṭubī invokes adherence to ʿUthmān's codex.

view: A reading of al-ʿaṣr with kasra on the ṣād is transmitted from Salām.
Ubayy reports reciting the sūra to the Prophet and asking him to interpret it.
A report identifies Abū Jahl with the person in loss and Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān and ʿAlī respectively with belief, righteous works, truth and patience.
note: The identifications are reported from the Prophet and repeated in a sermon by ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās.

view: Before accepting Islam, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ reportedly recited the short, eloquent sūra to Musaylima, who answered with an unimpressive parody about the wabr, a small catlike animal with notable ears.
note: Ibn Kathīr says even an idol-worshipper was not impressed and that al-Kharāʾiṭī recorded this or a close version in a book on bad character.

view: Two Companions reportedly recited Sūrat al-ʿAṣr to each other when meeting and exchanged greetings before parting.
note: Qutb says this renewed their commitment to its guidance.

view: Al-Shāfiʿī says reflection on this short sūra would suffice people; another saying holds that it gathers all Qur'anic sciences.
The sūra is Meccan.
note: Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Zubayr and most authorities support this; Ṭabāṭabāʾī finds it more likely than Medinan.

view: The sūra is Medinan.
note: Attributed to Mujāhid, Qatāda and Muqātil; Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows the possibility but favors Meccan.

view: The sūra was revealed shortly after Sūrat al-Sharḥ, sūra 94.
The Medina II verse division joins the oath to verse 2.
A German rendering of this verse follows Zirker's translation.
The verse's loss parallels Luke 9:24; the Syriac Peshitta uses ḥsar, cognate with Arabic khasira and khusr.
note: Attributed to Torrey.

view: Philippians 3:7–8 offers another comparison for loss.
Many Qur'anic uses of khasira or khusr refer to final loss; Q 79:12 gives an early Meccan parallel.
note: The collection of examples is attributed to Torrey.

view: Verses 2–3 parallel the fall and exception described in 95:5–6.
Human aging brings weakness and decline, but believers continue to receive credit for good deeds done in youth, strength and health, paralleling 95:4–6.
note: Attributed to Ibrāhīm.

view: Sūrat al-Tīn describes the body's condition while al-ʿAṣr describes the soul, resolving an apparent conflict between their accounts of human decline.
The preceding sūra's warning against rivalry and accumulation explains the loss here: fixation on immediate wealth wastes life and obscures future accountability.
note: Study Quran connects 102:8 with accountability for time.

view: This sūra distinguishes the believer's condition from the unbeliever's after the previous warning against rivalry and repeated threats.
Human loss joins earlier warnings about ignorance, injustice, ingratitude and the delusion that wealth grants immortality.
note: The note cites 100:6 and 104:3.

view: Q 104's contrast of worldly wealth with future damnation strengthens a commercial interpretation of the oath and human loss.
A reading of al-ʿaṣr as the time merchants count a day's earnings links the oath's profit image with final loss.
note: Attributed to Robinson.

view: The late-afternoon oath followed by rebuke and believers' exception forms a three-rhyme sūra; a hymn-like analysis of it is disputed.
note: Corpus Coranicum rejects Neuwirth's proposed hymn-like resonance.

view: The oath by time points to the changes, gains, harms and wonders it contains and draws attention to human gain or loss within it.
note: One explanation treats these events as signs of the Creator's power.

view: The oath honors time as a valuable blessing and warns that it consumes life unless people work toward reform through faith and good deeds.
Time's senses of restraint and bestowal support both the warning of loss and the exception of those who gain through faith and works.
The oath can encompass every sense of ʿaṣr, particularly the final era as time's afternoon and Muhammad's age.
Afternoon evokes humanity's late creation, the closing stage of life and sorrow at returning without gain.
note: This also relates the sūra to al-Takāthur.

view: The oath by the Prophetic age before the warning of loss carries special force because Muhammad's mission arose amid widespread ignorance, unbelief, injustice and religious disorder, calling humanity toward reform and salvation.
note: The notes mention the first revelation's command iqra on a Night of Power and a transformation from the middle ages to the last era.

view: The sūra's title and images present human salvation as extracting a lasting essence from transient life, just as pressing extracts an essence and ʿaṣr is the essence of time.
note: Biqaʿī also calls humankind the noblest, best-proportioned species.

view: The sūra begins with the ruined and then the saved because preventing harm precedes securing benefit.
The sūra's clauses map to knowledge of God and the afterlife, required and preparatory worship, and patience completing the effort to avoid doubt and harm.
Al-Ghazālī likens the Qur'an to a sea with six minerals: knowledge of God, His attributes and acts, the afterlife, worship, faith-threatening doubts, and lessons from the saved and ruined.
The basmala says everything perishes except God, whose mercy reaches all and whose completed gifts distinguish His chosen allies.
Across all ages the route out of loss is faith, righteous action and mutual counsel in truth and patience; the sūra presents this as the Muslim community's identity and function.
note: Qutb emphasizes a community that guards truth patiently.

view: The brief sūra compresses Islam's whole way of life and the Muslim community's role into a concise statement.
note: Qutb calls its expression inimitable; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says it gathers Qur'anic aims.

view: The sūra explains life's value and how its use can lead either to individual and collective salvation or to enduring punishment.
A poem by Mehmet Âkif Ersoy presents true faith, righteous conduct, truth and steadfastness as the sequence that saves humanity from loss.
Believers who perform righteous deeds are excepted from human loss.
note: Elmalılı's fuller account includes all four traits of verse 3.

view: Completing faith, righteous works and mutual counsel in truth and patience places one among the saved and leads to enduring Gardens.
note: Elmalılı calls these four traits complete faith.

view: True faith in the abiding God and good works for Him do not fail, whereas faith in falsehood and deeds springing from it vanish.
Believers who do good avoid loss when they leave no good undone by doing its opposite, or repent of doing so.
The generic expression for righteous works includes every commanded good deed and abstention from sin; the relative clause explains why the believers escape loss.
The exception separates those who lose from those untouched by loss.
Al-Ḥasan sees the exception after mention of Hell in another passage as parallel to the exception of believers from loss here.
A compared passage mentions faith and works, while al-ʿAṣr adds mutual counsel in truth and patience, preventing further loss of reward.
Belief and good action fulfill life's purpose: resisting Satan brings God's pleasure and Paradise, while surrendering to temptation forfeits an extraordinary favor.
Īmān derives from amn, with senses of granting peace, attesting, trusting and certain faith; God is called muʾmin because He grants safety to those seeking refuge.
note: Attributed to Farāhī; the note cites 106:4.

view: Religious faith is certainty joined to humility, trust and adherence: one accepts God's signs, commands and decisions and submits to Him.
note: Attributed to Farāhī.

view: Righteous deeds must follow and attest genuine faith; claims of inward faith or mere words can deceive, while conduct shows whether faith has taken root.
note: A cited address to professed believers calls for belief expressed in deeds (4:136); faith is called the foundation and works its explanation.

view: Ṣāliḥāt denotes actions enabling outward and inward, worldly and religious, individual and collective development toward human potential.
note: Attributed to Farāhī.

view: Righteous deeds accord with God's wise design for the world's purposeful collective order.
Mutual counsel requires following established truth and persevering both in obedience and against sins.
Sufis counsel being a child of the present moment, valuing it for afterlife good.
Those denying the afterlife also urge seizing the present, but aim at worldly pleasure rather than afterlife gain.
note: Elmalılı contrasts this use of time with the Sufi account.

view: People wrongly blame time for misfortune; a cited poem says people, not time itself, are corrupt.
An elegy depicts life deceiving people while death feeds on it and every breath weaves a shroud.
note: The elegy is for the author's teacher and Balkan War dead.

view: Affliction first reaches prophets, then saints and then the best people in descending order of spiritual excellence.
Affliction is God's whip driving servants toward Himself.
The loss warning can be heard against opponents' claim that Muhammad was the one in loss: the oath reverses their assumption.
Ibn ʿAbbās names ʿAlī and Salmān as examples among the saved, while Abū Jahl exemplifies the one in loss.
note: Ālūsī cautions that neither example is exclusive.

view: Lifespan diminishes each day; failing to earn obedience during it leads to the greatest loss, permanent punishment.
The account of decline can apply to human history as well as individuals: each generation falls a degree below its predecessor.
